extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a patent claim recites an abstract idea under MPEP §2106.04, including enumerated groupings of abstract ideas, sub-groupings, examples of both eligible and ineligible claim types, and examiner procedure for Step 2A (Prong One and Prong Two).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts – mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, mathematical calculations (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2), subsection I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations. The Court has identified concepts falling within this grouping (e.g., procedures for converting binary-coded decimal to binary; formulas for alarm limits; the Arrhenius equation; mathematical formula for hedging). When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, examiners should consider whether the claim recites a mathematical concept or merely limitations that are based on or involve a mathematical concept. A claim does not recite a mathematical concept if it is only based on or involves a mathematical concept (see Thales Visionix example). A mathematical concept need not be expressed in mathematical symbols; words operating on data to solve a problem can serve the same purpose. Examples of cases: Gottschalk v. Benson; Parker v. Flook; Diamond v. Diehr; Bilski v. Kappos; SAP America v. InvestPic; Digitech Image Techs. v. Elecs. for Imaging; Bancorp Servs. v. Sun Life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers. A mathematical relationship may be expressed in words or using mathematical symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples recited in claims: relationship between reaction rate and temperature (Arrhenius equation, Diamond v. Diehr); conversion between binary coded decimal and pure binary (Benson); mathematical relationship between directional radio activity and antenna conductor arrangement (Mackay Radio); organizing and manipulating information through mathematical correlations (Digitech). A relationship expressed in words can fall within this grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a numerical formula or equation will be considered as falling within the 'mathematical concepts' grouping. Textual formulations that replace symbols (e.g., 'determining a ratio of A to B') also fall here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: electromagnetic standing wave formula (Mackay Radio); the Arrhenius equation (Diehr); formula for computing an alarm limit (Parker v. Flook); mathematical formula for hedging (Bilski). A phrase that is a textual replacement for an equation (e.g., 'calculating force by multiplying mass by acceleration') should be treated as reciting the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a mathematical calculation, when given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification, will be considered as falling within the 'mathematical concepts' grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mathematical calculation is a mathematical operation (such as multiplication) or an act of calculating using mathematical methods to determine a variable or number. A claim need not use the word 'calculating' to be considered a calculation; terms like 'determining' a variable or 'performing' an operation may suffice. Examples: resampled statistical analysis to generate a distribution (SAP America v. Investpic); calculating an alarm limit (Parker v. Flook); converting geospatial coordinates to natural numbers; managing insurance policy values via calculations (Bancorp); algorithms for optimal visits (In re Maucorps); calculating differences between local and average data (In re Abele).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain methods of organizing human activity – fundamental economic principles or practices; commercial or legal interactions; managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2), subsection II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grouping covers concepts relating to economic/commercial/legal activities and interpersonal management. Not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract ideas (e.g., a defined set of steps for combining ingredients to create a drug formulation is not a 'certain' method). The grouping is limited to the enumerated sub-groupings and generally should not be expanded beyond them except in rare circumstances (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)). The sub-groupings encompass activity by a single person or multiple people, and activity between a person and a computer may fall within the grouping. The number of people involved is not dispositive; determination is based on whether the activity itself falls within a sub-grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices or principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental economic practices or principles include hedging, insurance, and mitigating risks; concepts relating to the economy and commerce may be considered 'fundamental economic practices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'fundamental' is not limited to old or well-known practices; new methods (e.g., price optimization) may be fundamental. Case examples: Bilski (hedging), Bancorp (insurance), OIP Technologies (price optimization), In re Smith (wagering game rules), In re Chorna (financial instruments). The Supreme Court treated intermediated settlement/risk hedging as a 'fundamental economic practice' (Alice). These practices have been found to be abstract ideas when claimed as a series of steps to implement them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial or legal interactions include agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: buySAFE v. Google – claims to a transaction performance guaranty (a contractual relationship) were characterized as reciting a commercial/legal interaction. Other examples include placing orders based on displayed market information, local processing of payments for remote purchases, using markings on mail to communicate sender/recipient/contents information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships (including social activities, teaching, following rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts directed to managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people, including social activities, teaching, and following rules or instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sub-grouping covers activities involving personal behavior and interpersonal interactions; such activity may be tied to a person-computer interaction (e.g., anonymous loan shopping via mobile phone) and may therefore fall within this grouping depending on the nature of the activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes – concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion) (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2), subsection III).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grouping captures concepts that can be performed entirely in the human mind or are mental steps such as observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion. When a claim limitation falls within this grouping, it may be a judicial exception absent additional claim elements that integrate the idea into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure for identifying abstract ideas (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim under examination that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas listed above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If identified limitation(s) falls within at least one grouping, it is reasonable to conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and the claim then requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, it is reasonable to find that the claim does not recite an abstract idea, concluding the judicial-exception eligibility analysis (claim eligible at Pathway B) unless the claim recites another exception (law of nature or natural phenomenon). Examiners should identify at least one abstract-idea grouping, and preferably identify all groupings to the extent possible if a limitation falls within multiple groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claims do not recite an abstract idea because they do not recite an abstract idea, even though at some level they may be based on or involve an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting hypothetical examples include: i) a printer comprising a belt, roller, printhead, ink cartridge; ii) a washing machine comprising tub, drive motor, controller, housing; iii) an earring with a sensor for blood glucose and memory; iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences (PCR amplification and sequencing); v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system (remote transfer to volatile memory and transferring control); vi) a method of rearranging GUI icons based on usage tracking and moving most used icons; vii) a method of training a neural network for facial detection using staged training sets. These are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B) because they do not recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope/limits of the 'certain methods' grouping and non-exhaustive nature of groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'certain' limits the 'methods of organizing human activity' grouping to the enumerated sub-groupings and the groupings are not mutually exclusive; some claim limitations may fall within multiple groupings or sub-groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract ideas (example: a defined set of steps for combining particular ingredients to create a drug formulation is not a 'certain' method of organizing human activity). The grouping should not be expanded beyond the enumerated sub-groupings except in rare circumstances (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)). If a claim limitation falls within multiple groupings, examiners should identify at least one, preferably all applicable groupings, and then proceed to analyze integration into a practical application in Step 2A Prong Two.
